metadata.title: Analysing ability grouping in secondary school: A way to improve academic performance and mitigate educational inequalities in Spain?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for Spain (15-year-old students) and constructs a treatment indicator (ABGROUP) from school-level questionnaire items. The analytic approach is Propensity Score Matching (PSM) with nearest-neighbour and exact matching, and outcomes are computed as differences in weighted means between matched treatment and control groups. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) in the matching or outcome estimation steps, so it is unclear whether complex survey design effects were incorporated. For replication with PISA Data, analysts should use the official PISA student sampling weights and, if available in the data product, replicate weights when estimating uncertainty for matched-group differences; otherwise, standard errors may be understated given the multistage sampling of students within schools.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA 2018 data for Spain only. Students with missing values on any analysed variables are eliminated from the sample (complete-case restriction). The treatment variable ABGROUP is defined for students enrolled in schools that apply ability grouping in all subjects (coded 1) versus only some subjects (coded 0). Students are then partitioned into three socio-educational vulnerability groups using the synthetic vulnerability index (SVI) based on percentile cut-points (below 25th, 25th–75th, above 75th), and PSM is performed separately within each vulnerability group.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Treatment vs control mean difference (t-test): High vulnerability: -0.88% (p<0.01, -2423**); Medium: -0.18% (not significant); Low: -0.26% (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Spain the study leveraged socio-educational vulnerability, ability grouping, and student background characteristics (e.g., repeating status, sex, and origin) to estimate the effect of ability grouping on global performance, finding that ability grouping produced a statistically significant decline for high-vulnerability students while medium- and low-vulnerability groups showed non-significant differences. This indicates that implementing ability grouping in Spain may worsen achievement outcomes for the most socio-educationally vulnerable students, undermining equity goals.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Treatment vs control mean difference (t-test): High vulnerability: -0.67% (p<0.01, -2.6590***); Medium: -0.01% (not significant); Low: +0.04% (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Spain the study leveraged socio-educational vulnerability, ability grouping, and key matching covariates (repeating status, sex, and origin) to estimate the effect of ability grouping on science performance, finding a statistically significant negative effect only for high-vulnerability students. This indicates that ability grouping is unlikely to improve science achievement for vulnerable learners and may instead deepen science-related inequities.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Treatment vs control mean difference (t-test): High vulnerability: -0.83% (p<0.05, -2.3861**); Medium: -0.37% (not significant); Low: -0.97% (p<0.05, -2.1836**).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Spain the study leveraged socio-educational vulnerability, ability grouping, and matching covariates (repeating status, sex, and origin) to estimate the effect of ability grouping on reading performance, finding statistically significant declines for both high- and low-vulnerability students while the medium-vulnerability group showed no significant effect. This indicates that ability grouping may harm reading achievement across parts of the vulnerability distribution, suggesting that reading-focused support and classroom diversity may be preferable to tracking-like practices.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Treatment vs control mean difference (t-test): High vulnerability: -0.50% (p<0.05, -2.0783**); Medium: +0.17% (not significant); Low: -0.07% (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Spain the study leveraged socio-educational vulnerability, ability grouping, and matching covariates (repeating status, sex, and origin) to estimate the effect of ability grouping on mathematics performance, finding a statistically significant negative effect for high-vulnerability students but no significant effects for medium- and low-vulnerability groups. This indicates that ability grouping may be counterproductive for improving mathematics outcomes among the most disadvantaged students, reinforcing the need for equity-oriented instructional strategies.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes the effects of ability grouping on achievement in Spain using PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students. It constructs a treatment indicator (ABGROUP) from school questionnaire items and builds a synthetic socio-educational vulnerability index (SVI), then splits students into low/medium/high vulnerability groups using percentile cut-points. Propensity Score Matching (nearest-neighbour with exact matching) is used to create balanced treatment and control groups, and outcomes are computed as differences in weighted means for PISA plausible-value achievement measures (global, science, reading, mathematics). Across domains, the results show predominantly adverse effects: high-vulnerability students experience statistically significant declines in global performance, science, reading, and mathematics, while medium-vulnerability effects are generally non-significant. Reading also shows significant declines for low-vulnerability students. Limitations include reliance on PISA’s ability-grouping questionnaire (no direct information on within- vs between-class implementation) and the absence of reported complex-survey weight handling in the matching/uncertainty estimation.
